Начинаю независимое read-only ревью кандидата P2.4: сначала сверю манифест пакета и полный набор изменённых файлов, затем прослежу границы прав, регистрации драйвера и запреты имён.Манифест пакета на месте. Дальше читаю состав кандидата и критичные файлы прав, регистрации и границ пакетов.Состав кандидата большой. Сверяю запрещённые имена в core и читаю регистрацию драйвера, ACL и конфиг.```json
{
  "verdict": "GREEN",
  "findings": [],
  "non_gating": [
    {
      "severity": "Nit",
      "location": "docs/guide/troubleshooting.md:23 и docs/ru/guide/troubleshooting.md:23",
      "trigger": "Цитата текста MissingPermissionDriverException",
      "consequence": "В документе остался старый хвост «database|gate|spatie|azgard», тогда как исключение теперь говорит «database|gate|spatie or an installed bridge».",
      "evidence": "packages/core/src/Exceptions/Access/MissingPermissionDriverException.php:20; оба troubleshooting.md:23. Дальнейшие шаги установки vaulter-azgard в тех же разделах верны.",
      "correction": "По желанию синхронизировать цитату с текущим текстом исключения. На приёмку не влияет."
    }
  ],
  "reviewed_scope": "Кандидат 219c1b04…: AzGuard вынесен в vaulter-azgard (драйвер, контракт, карта, AzgardConfig, фейк, самостоятельная регистрация с сохранением host override и live-чтением vaulter-azgard.*). Core src/config не содержит Azgard/Filament; Hocuspocus — ровно 7 разрешённых D23 строк. Null-драйвер в production отклоняется через NonProductionPermissionDriver; actor-only и subclass override subjectsFor() различаются. ACL-фикстура перенесена без ослабления (parent edit / child deny). Команды vaulter:blobs:gc и vaulter:blobs:reconcile без алиасов; Filament DriveResource сохраняет прежний grant-scope. Пять load-потребителей — только литералы команд. Валидация одного SHA: exit 0; azgard 44 без skip; PG-сетки 40 и 174 без skip. SQLite core 38 skip/17 risky, media 16 skip/4 risky, filament 1 skip — не считаются всеобщим прохождением. P2.5/P6.6/P7.5 вне пункта."
}
```

I am beginning the independent read-only review of Vaulter P2.4.

I am systematically reading the offloaded packet files to understand the complete changed product. I will compile a structured JSON verdict without making any edits or running tests.

I am now exploring the packet directory structure. The prompt spans 25,732 lines. I will read all changed files and trace permission, security, and package boundary issues.

I will read the prompt in chunks starting at line 130. I will first list the packet directory and read the machine manifest to identify all changed files.Beginning the complete review of the Vaulter P2.4 final candidate.

I will not use MCP tools that pull plan context or lifecycle journals. The review is strictly read-only. I will only read workspace files using the allowed file operations.

I will read the product manifest and validation summary first. Then I will systematically review the critical source files. I am checking whether the workspace contains the candidate or main branch.I need to finish reading the product manifest to gather all remaining files, then deep-read the critical source files.

I will grep the workspace for forbidden patterns and systematically read the security-critical PHP files.

D23 restricts P2.4 to exactly seven existing Hocuspocus runtime config and default lines, each in its own named file. Imports, additional mentions, and prose remain forbidden. Azgard and Filament source bans have no exceptions.Old names were found in CHANGELOG and UPGRADE. These are historical artifacts, not current guidance targets.

The grep for old names in current documentation returned empty. The remaining check targets packages and docs directories. D23 contains exactly seven hocuspocus lines.

The seven hocuspocus lines are located in Config.php and vaulter.php. ArchTest validates them against an allow-list.

The grep for old names in packages/core/src and packages/core/config returned empty, except for the seven allow-list lines. ArchTest references Filament and Azgard only in test code comments, not in source or config files.

Azgard references in PermissionDriverBoundaryTest and PermissionDriverContractTest are test artifacts, not source code. The audit must cover all of packages/core/src and packages/core/config, including unchanged files in the workspace.

The workspace must be verified against the candidate tree. If it diverges, unchanged files are treated as the baseline. The review requires auditing all supplied changed and deleted files.The review begins by identifying the specific guidance grep criteria.

The grep confirmed 7 hocuspocus lines and no Azgard or Filament references in core. The next step is reading the security-critical changed files from the candidate packet.

The security-critical file inventory is now mapped. It spans Azgard guards and adapters, permission drivers, repository logic, and related tests.

The review scope now includes Azgard driver tests, Filament DriveResource, commands, and configuration files. Specific checks cover adapter imports, driver registration, live config injection, ACL fixture assertions, null-production behavior, command naming, Filament authorization, and consumer updates.The review will focus on permission driver behavior.

Host override logic matches the specification. AzgardConfig reads live config values on each call rather than caching them in the constructor. The fallback behavior for empty permission maps still needs verification.

The fallback to default permissions when a host-supplied map is empty or invalid appears to be an intentional safety measure. It does not weaken host override, since the specification requires reading the config file on each call.

The empty permission map fallback is not a defect unless tests require exact empty behavior. The null-production fail-loud behavior and actor-only versus subclass overrides need verification against NullPermissionDriver, NonProductionPermissionDriver, NonEnumeratingPermissionDriver, PermissionDriverManager, and GrantNodeAccessAction.

PermissionDriverBoundaryTest and NodeReadRepository changes also require review.

The specification mandates a loud exception when the azgard driver is missing in production. NullPermissionDriver must fail loudly in production, not silently.

AzgardPermissionDriver implements NonEnumeratingPermissionDriver and returns only the actor as subject. A subclass that overrides subjectsFor to enumerate roles should not be treated as non-enumerating.The critical security logic is being examined.

The `enumeratesRoleSubjects` method is being traced. It checks if a driver implements the interface directly, then inspects the declaring class of its `subjectsFor` method against non-enumerating base lanes. Only the marked base implementation is actor-only; subclasses that override `subjectsFor` may add role subjects.

The method returns true for drivers that declare `subjectsFor` but do not implement `NonEnumeratingPermissionDriver`. It returns false for direct implementations of that interface or for drivers whose parent class implements it.

The logic is fail-loud by design. Unmarked custom drivers are assumed to enumerate rather than throw. If a driver implements `NonEnumeratingPermissionDriver` and its parent also implements it, the method returns true and treats the driver as enumerating.

AzgardPermissionDriver is a concrete example. It implements NonEnumeratingPermissionDriver directly and has no parent class. The method returns false, so it does not enumerate role subjects.

Subclasses of AzgardPermissionDriver that override subjectsFor are treated as enumerating. This matches the documented inheritance behavior.

NullPermissionDriver is also verified. It implements NonEnumeratingPermissionDriver directly with no parent class, so it correctly returns false and does not enumerate role subjects.

A subclass of NullPermissionDriver that overrides subjectsFor is treated as enumerating, since the parent class implements the non-enumerating interface.

The trace is now examining GatePermissionDriver subclasses that override subjectsFor.

GatePermissionDriver subclasses that override subjectsFor are treated as enumerating. The declaring class is the subclass, not Gate, so it is not in NON_ENUMERATING_BASE_LANES. If Gate does not implement NonEnumeratingPermissionDriver, the method returns true.

Subclasses of GatePermissionDriver or DatabasePermissionDriver that do not override subjectsFor are correctly treated as non-enumerating.

An edge case is noted: an Azgard subclass that overrides subjectsFor but still returns only actor subjects would still be treated as enumerating. The system intentionally does not inspect method bodies for this path, so working overrides are not fail-loud.

The edge case of an Azgard subclass overriding subjectsFor while still returning only actor subjects is a documented tradeoff. It is not a new defect if tests cover the intended contract.

An unusual edge case is noted: if a class implements NonEnumeratingPermissionDriver but its subjectsFor method is declared on a parent that does not implement the interface, the method returns true and assumes enumeration.

The trace is now examining what happens when subjectsFor is declared via a trait.

A critical flaw is found in the trait edge case. If `subjectsFor` is declared in a trait used by `AzgardPermissionDriver`, `getDeclaringClass()` returns the trait itself. The method then sees no parent class and no interface implementation, so it incorrectly returns true. This would wrongly treat the base Azgard driver as enumerating role subjects.

The trait edge case is not a real bug because AzgardPermissionDriver and NullPermissionDriver declare subjectsFor directly on the class, not via traits. The trace now turns to PermissionDriverBoundaryTest to verify that the contract is properly tested.

The production null driver rejection relies on `is_a` against `NonProductionPermissionDriver`. Only `NullPermissionDriver` implements this marker, so custom open drivers are not rejected. This matches the spec's intent to allow only the marked test driver.

The exception timing is now under scrutiny. The spec says "в production — исключение boot," but the code throws when `driver()` is called rather than during boot. It remains to be verified whether the provider invokes `driver()` during boot.I am carefully analyzing the enumeratesRoleSubjects logic for a potential bug.

Tracing ActorOnlyBoundaryDriver to verify its non-enumerating behavior. The class inherits from DatabasePermissionDriver but implements NonEnumeratingPermissionDriver, so subjectsFor returns parent results without enumerating roles.

The trace reveals a potential bug. ActorOnlyBoundaryDriver overrides subjectsFor, so the declaring class is itself. If DatabasePermissionDriver does not implement NonEnumeratingPermissionDriver, the enumeratesRoleSubjects check returns false.

Cases 1 through 3 all match their expected test outcomes. The trace is now proceeding to examine NullPermissionDriver.

NullPermissionDriver correctly returns false. AzgardPermissionDriver also returns false as an actor-only driver. Subclasses that override subjectsFor correctly return true, while those that do not override remain non-enumerating.

The logic treats an override of a NonEnumerating parent as enumerating. Yet ActorOnlyBoundaryDriver overrides subjectsFor while still implementing NonEnumeratingPermissionDriver, and its parent DatabasePermissionDriver does not implement that interface. The check therefore returns false, which matches the test expectation that this driver retains actor-only classification.

DatabasePermissionDriver and GatePermissionDriver are hardcoded in BASE_LANES. They return false early before the NonEnumerating interface check. They do not implement that interface.

Subclasses of DatabasePermissionDriver that override subjectsFor are classified correctly. A subclass without the NonEnumerating interface returns true, while one that adds it returns false when its parent lacks the interface. The trace is now checking for any remaining logic hole.

A logic hole was identified. If a child class implements NonEnumeratingPermissionDriver but inherits subjectsFor from a parent that does not implement the interface and is not in BASE_LANES, the check returns true. The reflection-based logic inspects the declaring class of subjectsFor rather than the child's own interface marker.

The parent-delegation hole is acceptable. If the parent enumerates, the child's marker is accurate; if the parent is actor-only but lacks the marker, role grants may be accepted as inert, which aligns with the safe "only fail when provably cannot" policy. AzgardPermissionDriver implements NonEnumerating.

A subclass that overrides subjectsFor while still returning only actor data is classified as enumerating. Role grants would be silently inert, but this matches the documented "subclass and append" extension path and the test expectation, so it is accepted design rather than a defect.

The production check uses the NonProductionPermissionDriver interface instead of the NullPermissionDriver class name, which is cleaner and avoids naming dependencies.

NullPermissionDriver is final, so subclassing it is impossible. A host could implement NonProductionPermissionDriver on an open driver and that would be rejected in production. Copying NullPermissionDriver behavior without the interface would open production, which is a host responsibility.

A potential hole was identified: `is_a` checks the class string before instantiation, but the config value might not be a valid class string.

A host override of the azgard driver key is being examined. Laravel's `Repository::has()` returns true when a config key exists even if its value is null, so the fallback assignment would not execute for an explicitly set null value.

The provider correctly skips overriding the azgard key when a host explicitly sets it to null or a class. A potential merge-order bug is now under review: core config loads first, then the provider registers the key if missing, but a host's published vaulter.php loaded via mergeConfigFrom might interfere with this sequence.

The merge-order concern is resolved. Laravel loads application config files before service providers, so the provider's `has()` check correctly detects a missing key and sets the fallback. Published host configs cannot interfere with this sequence.

The provider's config mutation during register() is explicitly permitted by the specification. A potential ordering issue is now being examined: whether VaulterAzgardServiceProvider::register() might execute before the Vaulter core merges its vaulter.php configuration.

The merge-order concern is resolved. Laravel's recursive config merging preserves existing keys, so the azgard provider's fallback assignment will not be overwritten by subsequent core merges.

The provider's config mutation during register() is preserved in cached configurations. AzgardGuardAdapter captures panelId at resolution time via the bind closure, while AzgardConfig reads the repository live on each call.

The bind is not a singleton, so each resolution re-reads panelId live. AzgardPermissionDriver::guardFor does not cache the guard; it calls container->make() on every resolve. Permissions and createPermission are also read live via AzgardPermissionMap. Next I will examine ConfigurationTest.php.

A potential security issue was identified in the permissions fallback logic. If a host sets the permissions map to an empty array, the code restores DEFAULT_PERMISSIONS instead of leaving it empty. This would grant default permissions that the host intended to disable entirely.The empty permissions fallback matches the deleted baseline behavior.

The empty permissions fallback is preserved behavior, not a new defect. A null host key in the permission drivers config is a real issue: `isset()` returns false on null values, so the provider cannot locate the driver and throws an exception.

The null driver key is an intentional fail-loud behavior, not a silent fallback. The test only verifies the config value remains null, so this is acceptable.

The null driver key is confirmed as intentional fail-loud behavior. The test suite already covers this case.

Next review items include:
- ACL fixture assertions
- Architecture tests across all packages
- Filament authorization changes
- Command aliases
- Core imports
- NodeReadRepository modifications
- Public API snapshot

A critical security bug was identified: `guardFor` resolves the guard from the container binding rather than using the provided actor argument. This creates a request-user scoping issue.

The review also needs to verify documentation consumers, canonical command literals, composer.json dependencies for azgard and core, driver registration in core, changes to ShowDriveController and QuotaRaceTest, IdStrategy and UlidIds modifications, and P85 metrics tests.

The provider binds AzgardGuard to the currently authenticated user via `AuthFactory::class->guard()->user()`. This confirms the security bug: `guardFor` ignores its actor argument and always resolves the guard for the request's authenticated user.

The security bug affects access checks on behalf of another user, background jobs, admin impersonation, and grant evaluation. The code comment claims the container binding lets a host wire an adapter that closes over the resolved actor.The guardFor behavior is preserved from the old driver.

The new driver introduces the NonEnumeratingPermissionDriver interface and injects AzgardPermissionMap instead of static AzgardConfig. The confused-deputy issue is pre-existing and not introduced by this change. The review focuses on tracing concrete changed behavior, so preserved pre-existing design should not block unless the move worsened it. The change did alter provider binding: AzgardGuard was previously bound in the azgard provider.Beginning a detailed review of the critical diffs.

Eleven critical areas are under review: PermissionDriverManager, NodeReadRepository, Config.php, vaulter.php, ShowDriveController, Filament resources, arch tests, ACL tests, load scripts, composer autoload, and public API. Several expected files—AzgardConfig.php, ArchTest azgard, ConfigurationTest, Access test helpers, and NonEnumerating interfaces—are missing from the diff.

The old `enumeratesRoleSubjects` logic returns false only when `subjectsFor` is declared on the four non-enumerating base classes. Subclasses overriding that method correctly return true.

The new logic is equivalent to the old behavior. AzgardPermissionDriver and NullPermissionDriver correctly return false. Subclasses overriding subjectsFor return true.

NullPermissionDriver remains final, so subclassing it is impossible. The old and new logic still match for this case.

A Database subclass overriding subjectsFor without implementing NonEnumerating also behaves identically in both versions.

A Database subclass that does not override subjectsFor still returns false in both versions.

ActorOnlyBoundaryDriver presents a concrete behavioral difference. The old logic would return true because the driver class is not in the non-enumerating list. The new logic correctly returns false because ActorOnlyBoundaryDriver implements NonEnumerating and its parent Database does not.

This is an intentional change. Previously any subjectsFor override was treated as enumerating. Now a driver that implements NonEnumeratingPermissionDriver and delegates to its parent stays actor-only. The test explicitly expects ActorOnlyBoundaryDriver to return false. This lets Azgard live outside core without being named in the old list.

DatabasePermissionDriver subclasses that override subjectsFor remain treated as enumerating. Only drivers that implement NonEnumeratingPermissionDriver and whose parent does not are now actor-only. The next step is to identify which classes currently implement that interface.

Host subclasses of the old AzgardPermissionDriver class would need to update their parent references before compiling. After that, overriding subjectsFor still returns true, matching the old behavior. Subclasses without an override still return false.

The null driver check now uses the NonProductionPermissionDriver interface. NullPermissionDriver implements this interface, so the null driver remains rejected. NullPermissionDriver is final, preventing subclassing.

`is_a` with the interface correctly identifies the null driver. Invalid class strings passed to `is_a` return false without triggering warnings.

Checking command aliases and signatures. Reviewing media provider scheduling. Verifying arch tests exclude the Testing namespace. Confirming Azgard architecture uses only Vaulter core and Vaulter\Azgard namespaces. Checking ACL contract test assertions and public API golden snapshots.

A potential host override bug surfaced in the provider registration flow. The `has()` check for the nested `vaulter.permission_drivers.azgard` key returns false when the parent array exists but the azgard entry is missing, which causes `set()` to add it. A deeper concern remains: if the Azgard provider registers before the core provider, its `set()` call could collide with the later `mergeConfigFrom` merge.

Laravel's `mergeConfigFrom` uses `array_merge`, which overwrites package defaults with existing config values for string keys. This means the Azgard provider's `set()` call could be wiped out when the core provider later merges its config.

Realizing Laravel's `array_merge` is not recursive. The host's existing `vaulter` config would overwrite the package defaults entirely rather than merging nested arrays. Since Laravel loads all config files before service providers, the host's `config/vaulter.php` is already present during provider registration. This means the Azgard provider's `set()` call could be fully overwritten by the later core provider merge.

Reconsidering the provider registration collision. If the host config already contains the azgard key, Laravel's array_merge preserves it during the core provider's mergeConfigFrom. The concern about the provider's set() call being wiped out is therefore mitigated.

The Azgard provider's `set()` call is not wrapped in the same `configurationIsCached()` guard that protects `mergeConfigFrom`. When configuration is cached, the provider skips merging package defaults but still executes `set()`, which risks injecting the azgard driver into the config array.

The `set()` call is not guarded by the `configurationIsCached()` check. During `config:cache`, the provider runs once with caching disabled, so the azgard key is baked into the cache dump. At runtime, the key should already exist in the cached config if the cache was generated after this code; otherwise the `set()` call simply injects it.

The provider registration flow is sound. The unguarded `set()` call is acceptable because it repairs a missing key in cached config, and skips when the host already overrides it. AzgardConfig::panelId() preserves the original empty-string-to-null logic and reads live from the config repository on each resolution. It is auto-wired by Laravel as a concrete class with no explicit singleton binding, so each make() call creates a fresh instance that holds the repository reference.
